cards.title: Program an LLM with competitor video transcripts to mine copy angles
cards.summary: Download a niche expert's video transcripts, feed them into an LLM, and prompt for angles, stories, common phrases, and audience-relatability hooks to speed up copywriting research.
cards.use_when: You need ad angles, email hooks or landing-page copy for a product in an unfamiliar niche and want to research a proven creator's messaging before writing.
steps: Pick 3-5 videos from a person who already sells successfully to your target audience. Open each video, click 'more' then 'show transcript' (interface may change - verify current steps), copy the full transcript, and paste it into ChatGPT or a similar LLM along with the other transcripts.

Program the model by telling it: 'These are transcripts of how this person talks and what they say.' Then request the specific outputs you need—angles to justify a claim, story ideas, and content blocks.

For faster research on any single video, ask the model to: distill the video into a few paragraphs with the most important points; list common phrases used; identify any core message; describe any stories (what happened, who was involved); and flag places where the speaker relates to the audience by demonstrating they understand what the audience thinks and why.

Seed your own copy with the mined material: reuse the speaker's hooks, common sayings and offer logic, but substitute your product's specifics. You can have access to the exact same document with prompts and email templates inside a free copy starter kit.
Note that an 17-minute video can be summarized in about 30 seconds this way, making copying research efficient.
caveats: Efficiency is the relationship between effort and output—high input with low output wastes time. Reuse ideas, not the exact words, when adapting the material to your own product.
The LLM is only as useful as the transcripts you feed it; you must still verify the niche, offer and audience yourself.

cards.title: Map why your list is on your list before emailing
cards.summary: Segment email subscribers by acquisition source—newsletter opt-in, free lead magnet, or past buyer—because each group expects different content and offers.
cards.use_when: You are planning an email sequence, welcome flow or promotion and need to decide what message each segment of your list should receive.
steps: List every way a subscriber can join your list. Typical sources: a newsletter opt-in where people want entertainment and exclusivity; a free lead magnet where they traded an email for a specific download or tool; and previous buyers who already trusted you enough to pay.

For each source, write down what the person expects: newsletter subscribers want to hear exclusive insights and stay up to date; lead-magnet subscribers want the promised specific outcome; customers want more of what they bought and complementary offers.

Match the offer and angle to the segment. Do not send a hard sales email to newsletter subscribers who signed up for entertainment, and do not send generic nurture to buyers who are ready for the next-step offer.
If you run different offers for different businesses or lead magnets, keep separate sequences per offer rather than one blended list.
caveats: Source-specific example: real-estate creator Hamza Ali's newsletter subscribers opted in for exclusive flex-space insights, so his emails sold more insights rather than a cold pitch.
This is a structural framework from the source's experience, not a tested benchmark; adapt to your own lists.

cards.title: Fill a prospect profile by watching their content
cards.summary: Compile a creator's captions, hooks, sayings, angles, offer and stories so you can write copy that sounds and reasons like them before you write a single line for them.
cards.use_when: You are writing ads, emails or landing pages for a brand or creator whose voice and offer you need to absorb quickly.
steps: Create a single document. Paste in several Instagram captions or other posts verbatim, plus transcripts of a few videos.

Write down what the offer actually is in plain terms. The source learned that flex space means office warehouses rented to offices, warehouses, retail or restaurants—you cannot write about an offer you don't understand.
Add a section for hooks: copy the exact opening lines that made you stop scrolling.
Add a section for common sayings and recurring phrases that sound like the person.
Add a section for angles and justifications: the arguments they repeatedly use to make their offer the obvious choice.
Add a section for stories: what happened, who was involved and how the story resolved. Stories need a main lesson at the end for readers to take away.

Add a section for audience relatability: lines that prove the speaker understands what the audience thinks and why. Example from the real-estate reel: 'if you're done with problematic tenants and 2 a.m. maintenance calls, I get it.'
Use this profile as the source of truth when drafting copy for that brand so the output matches their voice and logic instead of generic marketing language.
caveats: The document is a research asset, not a script—steal the ideas and structure, not the exact words.
Source demonstrates this process on a real-estate creator; verify the offer details yourself rather than assuming.

cards.title: Structure a first marketing email as a story with a delayed reveal
cards.summary: A proven email flow: state the problem, hint at what you'll show, go deeper on the problem, describe your experience with the solution, then reveal what it is and give one CTA.
cards.use_when: You need to write a promotional email that moves readers from problem awareness to a click without sounding like an ad.
steps: Open with a hook tied to the reader's current pain. Example structure used: 'Why I sold my residential properties and after hearing this you might too.'

Relate to the reader's desired outcomes (freedom, passive income, tax benefits) and then challenge them: 'I soon came to realize real estate provides almost none of those things at least if you follow how everyone else does it or how everyone else teaches it.'
Deepen the problem with concrete, specific pain points a real person recognizes—2 a.m. phone calls to fix broken toilets, tenants avoiding rent, the stress of finding deals.

Describe your own experience with the solution without naming it yet: 'I tried something new and instantly it was like a breath of fresh air.' Stay intriguing: don't reveal the answer in the sentence right after the tease.
Reveal what it is only after describing your experience and why it's better—the source flips the common order of naming the product first and praising it after.
End with one clear CTA and an offer. Example: 'if you want to learn how click here to join the flex space Network.'
Add situational urgency only where true, e.g. 'the opportunity probably won't be as accessible to beginners in a few years.'
caveats: The source's example sells a specific program at over seven figures per development—results are the source's anecdote, not a guarantee for your product.
Delaying the reveal only works if the payoff delivers real value; otherwise it reads as clickbait.

cards.title: Show why you're convinced instead of convincing readers
cards.summary: Persuasion friction drops when you demonstrate your own conviction and reasoning rather than repeatedly telling people they should buy.
cards.use_when: You are writing ad copy, emails or a sales page and catch yourself using pressure language like 'you need to get in before it's too late.'
steps: Replace imperative claims with personal conviction. Instead of 'you need to get into X before the opportunity is too late,' write why you yourself went all in while the opportunity was there.
Add a reflective regret frame: name opportunities you watched pass by while others made money and you sat on the sidelines. This gives the reader a concrete emotional picture without attacking them.
Tie the conviction to real, checkable reasoning—specific benefits, timing or mechanics you believe in.
Use the conviction to create situational urgency: real constraints like 'when I got in the opportunity was still there, but maybe not forever' rather than manufactured deadlines.
Keep the tone like a friend talking to a friend, not an exam paper. Short, punchy, to the point.
caveats: Conviction framing is the source's opinion and technique; it is not a universal rule that pressure never works.
Situational urgency must be genuine, or it becomes the same clickbait problem it is meant to avoid.

cards.title: Apply the four-part copy formula to every asset
cards.summary: Every piece of copy—email, ad, sales page—needs attention, consumption, persuasion, and action, and the beginning deserves the most effort.
cards.use_when: You are drafting, reviewing or diagnosing any ad, email, landing page or VSL and need a checklist for what might be missing.
steps: Attention: get past the brain's 'spam filter.' Write the hook or headline first and spend disproportionate time on it—successful YouTubers and advertisers spend most of their effort on title, thumbnail and first 10 seconds because nothing else matters if the reader never starts.
Consumption: make the copy easy and intriguing to read. If it isn't consumable, message quality is irrelevant.
Persuasion: shift the reader's beliefs in your favor—this is how selling works over time.
Action: end with an effective call to action.

When an asset underperforms, score it against these four; the weakest stage is usually the one to rewrite. The example hook in the source is a short, no-wasted-words scenario: 'I tied up an FBI agent and have $1,000 in this bag—here's a knife, good luck.'
caveats: The four-part formula is a rule of thumb from the source, not a guaranteed conversion driver.
Attention-getting hooks that don't lead to consumable, value-delivering copy break at stages two and three.

cards.title: Make a non-spammy promise and set the right consumption effort
cards.summary: Grab attention by decreasing the effort required to read while increasing intrigue; promises must be exciting but not spammy or platform-noncompliant.
cards.use_when: You are writing ad hooks, email subject lines, or landing-page headlines and need to be exciting without triggering spam filters or ad rejections.
steps: Lower consumption effort: write lean, short, punchy copy without fluff. Long intros that buries the point and aren't interesting get abandoned.
Raise intrigue: give hints the reader cannot guess. The source compares it to a guessing game—'guess what we're eating today,' then 'it starts with an m'—each wrong guess makes them more invested.

Make a promise that isn't spammy. Instead of 'make $10,000 in 20 days $$$,' write an exciting specific benefit the reader will get if they read on. Spammy wording can send email to the spam folder: the source cites open rates dropping from 25-30% to about 5% or less when messages land in spam.
Stay platform-compliant. Meta (Facebook) and Gmail enforce content rules; copy that even looks spammy can get an ad account shut down. Be honest like you're talking to a friend.
Add emotion without clickbait: use high-tension, surprising moments but always tie the payoff to real value so readers don't feel cheated.
caveats: The open-rate figures (25-30% vs 5%) are the source's illustrative numbers, not a controlled benchmark.
Platform rules change—verify current Gmail and Meta advertising policies before relying on claims.

cards.title: Use three-part attention formula: promise, intrigue, emotion
cards.summary: Grab reader attention by combining a non-spammy promise, non-confusing intrigue, and emotional drama with a real payoff instead of clickbait.
cards.use_when: You are crafting hooks for social ads, email subject lines, or opening paragraphs and need them to stop the scroll.
steps: Promise (not spammy): tell readers something amazing they will get if they keep reading. Example from the source: 'this is the coolest game ever—you can fly around and fight dragons' rather than just 'it's fun.' Keep claims honest enough to be compliant.

Intrigue (not confusing): make readers curious without confusing them. Confusion kills reading—if readers have to jump around or decode jargon they stop. Avoid over-technical language even when writing to smart business owners, because easy-to-digest messages reach both weaker and stronger readers.

Intrigue technique: build up in steps. Example: 'double your Instagram followers in 4 months without spending a dime—here's how I did it. First you need to understand the power of engaging content—but it's not just any content. There's a special type of post that gets 7-10 times more engagement than regular posts. No, it's not reels, carousels or single photos.' Then end with the payoff and a click.

Emotion (not clickbait): use dramatic hooks and suspense. Example: 'I'm quitting copywriting and starting drop shipping—here's why.' Build suspense ('I've heard beginners say this over and over'), then reveal the twist (you tried it and didn't quit).
Verify the emotional promise matches the content. Clickbait is a subject line or thumbnail that doesn't match what's inside—even if value exists, readers feel cheated.
Contrarian framing: challenge a commonly held belief (the source calls this the 'big challenge') to generate interest from people who want to know why you disagree.
caveats: The 7-10x engagement figure is the source's claim about a specific post type, not a general benchmark.
Contrarian disagreement draws attention but risks alienating the audience if the position isn't backed by real reasoning or value.

cards.title: Optimize for short attention spans by maximizing value per minute
cards.summary: Write for 'TikTok brain' by valuing value per minute over total value, using short sentences, bullets, visuals and a direct CTA.
cards.use_when: You are writing emails, PDP copy, ad creative or landing pages for an audience that scrolls short-form content.
steps: Judge copy by value delivered per minute, not total volume. The source argues a 200-word email with high value beats a 10,000-word email stuffed with value, because nobody will read the long one.
Start with a strong hook: e.g. 'Add 2 inches to your biceps in just 90 days—here's how' is specific about who and what; 'grow your arms' is vague and not fresh.
Use short sentences and paragraphs to stay simple and direct.

Use bullets and lists to pack maximum value into the most scannable format. Example bullets: 'lift heavy weights; eat 1g of protein per pound of body weight daily; get eight hours of sleep each night.'
Use visuals sparingly: one or two emojis in an email, more allowed in a caption, to convey emotion or point attention to your single biggest lesson.
Be direct—skip fluff and tell readers exactly what to do, like 'consume a protein shake within 30 minutes after your workout.'
End with a clear call to action, e.g. 'download the free 90-day arm building plan.'
caveats: The 200 vs 10,000-word comparison is the source's illustration, not a measured outcome.
Emoji and visual density should fit the channel—overloading an email with emojis looks unprofessional.

cards.title: Vary pacing like an action movie to hold attention
cards.summary: Alternate slow, explanatory passages with short, fast, exciting lines so copy has natural rhythm instead of being all slow or all fast.
cards.use_when: You are editing an email, sales page or VSL script that feels flat, chunky or exhausting to read.
steps: Recognize the two failure modes: all fast (nothing but fight scenes gets boring) and all slow (exposition with no action gets boring). Good copy alternates, like a roller coaster.

Slow down to explain when you need clarity: use longer sentences and more detailed explanation for the core teaching. Example: 'To build muscle effectively you need to understand the role of protein in muscle repair and growth.'
Don't over-explain. Avoid diving into protein synthesis and ratios—that reads like a study and bores readers. Sprinkle small short items (bullets) within explanations to keep pace.
Speed up to excite with short punchy sentences. Example recap: 'Lift heavy. Eat right. Sleep well. Watch your muscles grow.' Use this for recapping the main lesson at the end of an email.
Mix it up: alternate slow and fast cadences to create natural flow. Example: 'Building muscle isn't just about lifting weights—it's about strategy. Random lifting wastes time.'
Use transitional phrases to move smoothly between paces, e.g. 'now that you know the basics, let's get to the fun part.'

Avoid long blocks of text at the top of an email followed by short lines at the bottom—that kills pacing. Spaced, uneven line lengths read more easily than big chunky paragraphs, which look like a book people don't want to read.
caveats: Pacing advice is a stylistic principle from the source, not a tested conversion lift.
Specific examples use fitness copy—substitute your own vertical's language.

cards.title: Shift limiting beliefs before pitching the offer
cards.summary: People already know what to do; their limiting beliefs stop them, so prove you understand the belief, disprove it, install the new belief, then sell using it.
cards.use_when: You are writing a sales page, VSL or email and the audience resists buying despite knowing the general solution exists.
steps: Identify the desire and the limiting belief blocking it. Desires like 'lose weight and get in shape' are blocked by beliefs like 'healthy food is expensive,' 'I'm big boned,' 'my genetics are bad,' 'I'm too busy.'

Write value at the 'how' level, not the 'what' level. 'Eat less, burn more, go to the gym consistently' is something people already know, so it isn't valuable. Write 'how to curb cravings,' 'how fasting helps you eat less while staying full,' 'the best routine to do at the gym,' 'how to stay consistent.'

Follow the belief-shift sequence: (1) state the limiting belief in the reader's own words—'I can't lose weight because I hate being hungry'; (2) challenge it—'starving yourself and being hungry all the time isn't the answer'; (3) sympathize—'most people are told less calories equals less weight but they've been lied to'; (4) disprove the old belief with a concrete failure mode—hunger leads to binge cycles and is terrible for weight loss; (5) install the new belief—'losing weight is about strategic ways to stay full throughout the day while eating less calories'; (6) sell from the new belief—'if you want a meal plan built around your time and taste preferences click here.'

Support the new belief with proof: the source pairs the claim with side-by-side meal comparisons showing a homemade stuffed-crust pizza at 900 calories and 80g protein versus fast food with more calories, less protein, and triple the fat.
caveats: The nutrition macro figures are illustrations from the source's example, not verified data—verify any such claims before using them in your own copy.
Correcting people directly ('1+1=3, wrong') causes friction and defensiveness; understanding framing ('I see how you could think that—I thought so too until...') is more effective.

cards.title: Submit evidence strong enough that belief follows
cards.summary: You cannot force belief by demanding it; you must submit evidence strong enough that holding the belief becomes difficult, using analogies, quotes, statistics, cost narration, hypotheticals, and borrowed authority.
cards.use_when: You are writing a sales page, VSL, or ad that asks the reader to change how they see a product category or make a claim they may doubt.
steps: Use analogies to map the unfamiliar onto the familiar: 'a computer is like a brain because it processes information.' Apply the same to your mechanism or offer.
Use quotes to provide authoritative support and emotional resonance for an idea, raising credibility.
Use statistics to give concrete, factual evidence that supports your claim and builds trust. Verify any statistic before publishing.

Use cost narration to demonstrate the significant effort or investment behind your claim or knowledge—this shows value and credibility. Example: explaining how much research or iteration went into your method or product.
Use hypothetical examples to show how your concept plays out in real-life situations, making outcomes visual and relatable.
Use borrowed authority, like quotes, to leverage the credibility of experts or respected sources and transfer trust to your argument.

The framing exercise: you can't truly choose a belief without evidence. A kidnapper demanding you believe he's Jesus won't work—but if he turns water to wine, walks on water, and splits the sea, belief becomes almost unavoidable. Write copy that supplies that level of evidence for your claim.
caveats: This is a persuasion philosophy from the source, not a measured framework.
Manufacturing false proof or unverified statistics violates the honest-promise principle and can breach ad platform rules.
